newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cash crude diffs ease as futures rise.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cash crude diffs ease as futures rise.

text.p: U.S. cash crude differentials generally eased on Thursday as traders talked of an ample supply, even though benchmark West Texas Intermediate/Cushing prices rose sharply.

The WTI/Cushing price was driven up to $21.10/20 by late in the session compared with late Wednesday's $20.65/75, partly by a technical move on the futures market but also propped up by firm July exchange-for-physicals (EFPs) premiums.

The futures market bounced strongly when an early move to push it lower was met by large-volume short-covering. Meanwhile, EFP premiums remained offered up at 15 cents in anticipation of another month of heavy foreign crude delivery as traders play "pass-the-parcel" with the bulk of the more than two million barrels of Nigerian Bonny Light which was delivered on the June contract.
But traders said that the underlying fundamentals in the market pointed to weaker prices, as evidenced by thin trading acitivity and weaker grade differentials.

Among Thursday's few deals was a Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James (LLS) piece at an eight cent discount to WTI, West Texas Sour/Midland (WTS) transactions at $1.55 and $1.54 discounts and West Texas Intermediate/Midland at 35 cents under WTI.
LLS has been sagging for more than a week and traded at evens on May 19 and other grades have similarly been showing weakness.

Activity is mainly trading houses and refiners usually don't get into the market until the early part of a new month following the expire of futures and pipeline scheduling. The "swamp" grades -- Eugene Island, Bonita and Heavy Louisiana Sweet/Empire -- are usually traded only by refiners and seeing very little interest, brokers said.

Market participants noted that, even though data showed refinery runs in the U.S. were up 100,000 barrels per day last week, storage tanks in the Gulf and around the pipeline hubs were full up and inventories rose by more than 1.3 million barrels.
